Content:
I would argue that the fact that the trail the hikers were on was popular and hikers there were relatively common (for Siberia) lends _more_ credit to the Novichok hypothesis rather than less, if we assume it was a _deliberate,_ secret, open air nerve gas test of the newly developed Novichok by the FSB. It was 1993, the post-Cold-War post-Soviet era in Russia, a time of chaos ad corruption by oligarchs, a decade during which former KGB officer Putin slowly rose to power and the military and secret service agencies were looking for new narratives about "enemies from within and without". Putin found them in "domestic terrorists" (or freedom fighters, depending on the viewpoint) in former Soviet republics torn by civil war for independence. It's highly likely that the infamous nerve gas attack on an opera house in Moscow that killed so many people was also a test of the new Novichok by the FSB, on their own citizens, to test it and also be able to claim that Russia was under attack by terrorists. Doctors at the time quickly determined it must be some sort of toxic nerve agent, but couldn't identify it, as it was a new and unknown to them chemical.

While the KGB (the Soviet secret service) was dissolved after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, its successor the FSB (the Russian domestic intelligence service, which took over most of the former KGB's tasks, such as domestic espionage and state security, with the exception of foreign espionage).

When he says "Some parts of Northern Siberia have population density less than one person per square kilometer," I feel I must underscore just *how much* less. The Olenyoksky District in the Evenki part of Yakutia (the Sakha Republic) is 2/3 the size of the Yukon and, with 1/10 its population, has a density of 0.013 per square km.

Now, in Russia's 2010 census, Olenyoksky had a population of 4,127. It has four villages: Eyik, Kharyyalakh, Olenyok, and Zhilinda. Guess what the sum of their populations is.

Author: @blondbraid7986
Content:
What gets me about the testimony of Valentina, the sole survivor, is that in her first statement to the police, she described her group resting in their sleeping bags and just not waking up, something that is plausible with overexertion and hypothermia, and it was only years later in an 2018 interview that she described it as a sudden attack with blood and strange seizures.

The sources themselves are also conflicting, with some describe the girl covered in blood, but several other described her looking physically normal, but being unresponsive and staring into space.

We ought to remember that human memories can change over time, and especially with trauma, and wanting to find meaning in terrible things. I don't find it unlikely that she in her grief didn't want to believe that it was simply poor planning from her team leader, so her mind twisted the memories into a strange alien horror where her friends died trying to help each other, and one of the boys died while trying to save her, making their deaths almost heroic rather than just a sad accident.
